title: The Job Title Changed; The Knot in Your Stomach Didn't https://www.theartofaskingquestions.com/p/the-job-title-changed-the-knot-in-your-stomach-did-not
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (www.theartofaskingquestions.com), October 11, 2026
summary: Andrea Chiarelli adapts a piece first written in Italian with Marica Carrone about the anticlimax that follows a long-awaited promotion. A client finally received the title, the bigger team and the salary she wanted, yet woke up the next day with the same knot in her stomach. Chiarelli explains the feeling through Daniel Gilbert's research on the impact bias, in which professors who won tenure were no happier than those denied it, and argues that many career milestones are really attempts to answer an unanswerable question about whether the career is worth continuing. Using Sheldon and Elliot's self-concordance model, she shows that goals chosen to quiet self-doubt deliver far less satisfaction than goals that fit our own values. She ends with an acid test for any recent success: if you could achieve the same milestone again, would you still want it as much?
points: The flat feeling after a promotion is an ordinary forecasting error known as the impact bias, not evidence that you chose the wrong job.
Milestones pursued to prove yourself never settle the underlying doubt, so the relief wears off and the need moves on to the next goal.
Goals taken on to win an argument with yourself deliver much less than goals that fit your interests and values, according to the self-concordance model.
The acid test is to ask whether you would want the same achievement again, and a no or a maybe means the goal answered something other than a real need.
The client in the story did not quit, but she began choosing goals by asking what she wanted to build without having to convince anyone.
quotes: The anticlimax after a promotion isn’t a sign that we chose the wrong job, but a fairly ordinary error in how we forecast our own feelings.

Psychologists call this the impact bias. We are reasonably good at predicting whether something will feel good or bad, and much worse at predicting how strongly it will land and how long the feeling will last.
The point is that many of the milestones you chase are trying to answer one question: whether it is still worth carrying on with that career you chose years ago.
Live like this and you stop distinguishing between what you really want and what you would need as proof. You choose each new goal not for its own worth but for how effectively it silences the doubt.
reaching a goal we took on to settle an argument with ourselves does much less for us than reaching one we actually wanted.
Take your most recent professional success and ask yourself: If I were to achieve exactly the same milestone again, would I still want it as much?
What do I really want to build for myself, without the stress of having to convince anyone, myself included?
